description: We are beginners, this is our first hackathon. We will win.
summary:
Ares Path — Plan Your Journey Across Mars

Ares Path is an interactive Marswalk planning platform designed to help future explorers plan scientific excursions across Jezero Crater.

The platform brings together Martian terrain imagery, environmental information, science destinations, and route-planning tools in a single interface. Explorers can investigate potential destinations, compare routes, estimate travel time and energy requirements, and explore simulated mission scenarios.

Our goal is to transform complex planetary information into a more accessible exploration-planning experience.

Ares Path is a prototype intended for educational and mission-planning demonstrations, not an operational astronaut navigation system.
details:
Ares Path is an interactive Mars exploration website developed for “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map.” It explores a practical question: Which science destination can an explorer visit, how should they approach it, and can they return within their available time and resources?

Our prototype focuses on a bounded region of Jezero Crater. Its guided demonstration proposes a hypothetical visual survey near the western fan front and Three Forks, using a published USGS coordinate and a fictional starting habitat.

What it does and how it works

Ares Path combines optical imagery, elevation, thermal infrared, spectral information and geological context. Users can place a habitat and destination, add or remove waypoints, and mark exclusion zones. A deterministic A* pathfinding algorithm generates alternatives that prioritize shorter distance, a balance between distance and slope, or gentler terrain.

The map displays these alternatives together with matching colours and comparison tables. In our reproducible example, the balanced route reduces the maximum modeled slope from approximately 5.4° to 2.9°, while adding approximately 0.65 km to the return journey, 24 minutes of allocated time and 36 Wh of estimated rover energy. This makes the tradeoff visible instead of presenting one route as universally best.

The Mission Simulator checks time allocation and a hypothetical support rover’s battery reserve. Ares Experience lets users follow their selected route through an educational terrain simulation. A separate view displays real Perseverance photography. Supporting tools include historical Mars observations and an experimental AI4Mars-trained terrain segmentation viewer.

Benefits and intended impact

The project brings information from multiple missions into one understandable planning workflow. Users can connect a scientific objective to terrain constraints and see how their choices affect distance, time and energy.

Our intended impact is educational: helping students and space enthusiasts understand the decisions behind surface exploration. The prototype also demonstrates how transparent, reproducible calculations could support the development of more advanced mission-planning tools.

Tools and technologies

We used HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the interface, Canvas and WebGL for interactive views, and a Cloudflare Worker backend on ChatGPT Sites for calculation APIs. We prepared a Node.js adapter for Vercel migration. Ares Vision uses ONNX Runtime Web.

Scientific inputs include MRO CTX imagery and stereo elevation, Mars Odyssey THEMIS thermal imagery, MRO CRISM spectral data, and USGS geological mapping. GitHub supports source sharing. We used OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex assistance for development, debugging and documentation. The homepage artwork is AI-generated and visibly labelled. No specialized hardware was required.

Creativity and factors we considered

Ares Path connects scientific context, route comparison, resource calculations and route playback in one guided experience. Its emphasis is on explaining why alternatives differ.

Our team considered beginner usability, readable legends, data coverage, source attribution, terrain resolution and uncertainty. We distinguish observations from model estimates and hypothetical scenarios. Current local weather, radiation, fine obstacles, traction and spacesuit consumables remain unresolved. A route that fits the configured budgets does not establish real-world safety or authorize an astronaut excursion.
